newsitem.title: USA: Cleveland voters reject tax abatement restrictions.
newsitem.headline: Cleveland voters reject tax abatement restrictions.

text.p: - Cleveland residents decided not to be the first in the country to limit local government's ability to offer tax breaks to business when they voted Tuesday to reject a referendum that would have limited the impact of tax abatements on new construction.
Had the issue passed, it would have been the first time anywhere in the United States that a city chose to preserve school funding at the expense of tax abatements.

Voters turned down a ballot referendum proposed by school teachers that would have made it harder for the city to offer businesses tax abatements. These abatements, the teachers say, cost the schools millions of dollars annually in property tax revenue.

In Ohio, school districts are independent from local government and rely heavily on property taxes voted by residents of the school districts. But city and county governments can abate, or decrease, the amount of taxes paid on new construction -- either new homes, office buildings or factories.

The tax abatements apply not only to taxes levied by the municipal governments granting the abatements, but also by the independent school districts, which levy 60 percent of all property taxes in the state.

Cities use abatements to attract new businesses and retain expanding ones. Teachers argue that wealthy corporations are being given tax breaks at the expense of an impoverished school district. Property taxes provide approximately 45 percent of school system's $511 million budget. State and federal also support the schools.

Believing that tax abatements were costing the financially pressed Cleveland School District $21 million a year, the 5,000-member Cleveland Teachers Union proposed a referendum that would have had either the municipality or the entity receiving tax abatement, compensate the Cleveland schools for property tax revenues lost through the abatement.
In a light turnout, voters rejected the referendum with 15,421 voting for the referendum and 21,189 against, with 99.5 percent of precincts reporting.
The turnout of less than 37,000 was only 12.5 percent of the county's 297,000 voters, unusually low even for an August special election.

The issue's opponents, including Cleveland Mayor Michael White, argued that the issue's passage would have caused businesses to leave or bypass Cleveland, meaning that new workers would not be paying income taxes that benefit the city and the schools.
